paragraphs: Differential privacy can protect a numerical query by adding random noise to its answer. The central tradeoff is how much accuracy must be sacrificed for a given privacy guarantee. This paper examines whether the widely used Gaussian noise distribution is the best choice when the answer contains many coordinates.

The authors show that, as the number of dimensions grows without bound, no additive noise mechanism can asymptotically improve on the Gaussian mechanism’s privacy–utility tradeoff in the strong privacy settings they study. The result gives a theoretical justification for Gaussian noise, with its scope tied to both the high-dimensional limit and those privacy settings.

For certain low-dimensional settings, however, the authors identify better alternatives within a family called Spherical Generalized Gamma mechanisms. This family includes Gaussian noise and the existing l2 mechanism. They also establish tight composition results across the family, describing privacy behavior when mechanisms are combined. Together, the findings distinguish where Gaussian noise has an optimality justification from where other distributions can improve utility.
icml-2026-asymptotic-optimality-of-the-h.tldr: Gaussian noise is asymptotically optimal among additive noise mechanisms in the studied strong-privacy regime, while new mechanisms improve certain low-dimensional cases.

paragraphs: An agent can predict its next observation or perform a task successfully without having a broadly useful understanding of its environment. This paper argues that world-model evaluations should also ask questions about overall structure and hypothetical changes. Such questions test whether knowledge gained through interaction supports reasoning beyond the particular trajectories observed.

The proposed WorldTest protocol evaluates multiple environment-level queries, including whether states are reachable and what interventions would change. Individual queries can depend on properties that no single rollout distribution determines. Testing several query types together assesses whether a learned model supports different uses, rather than measuring success on one narrow prediction problem.

The authors implement the protocol as AutumnBench, containing 43 interactive grid worlds and 129 tasks across three query families. In experiments with 517 human participants and five frontier models, humans substantially outperform the models. The authors attribute this gap to differences in exploration and belief updating, pointing to how agents gather evidence and revise their understanding as important parts of world-model learning.
icml-2026-benchmarking-world-model-learn.tldr: WorldTest evaluates broad environmental understanding, and its AutumnBench implementation reveals a substantial human advantage over five frontier models.

paragraphs: Zero-shot imitation asks an agent to reproduce expert behavior from one demonstration, without further environment interaction or parameter updates at test time. CIRL approaches this by treating many tasks as attempts to reach a particular goal state. Inferring that goal can make interpreting a demonstration more tractable than recovering an unrestricted reward function.

During pretraining, the framework learns without rewards or demonstrations. It combines a contrastive method for learning maximum-entropy goal-conditioned policies, an automatic goal proposal mechanism called GoalKDE that encourages exploration, and a variational model that infers goals from trajectories. These components connect learning how to reach states with learning how to interpret observed behavior.

The theoretical result establishes consistent recovery of demonstrator intent while accounting for differences in how difficult states are to reach. The authors also explain why structurally similar approaches can infer the wrong reward. Experiments on both goal-conditioned and standard reward-maximizing control tasks outperform prior zero-shot imitation methods, supporting goal states as useful compact descriptions of behavior across the tested tasks.
icml-2026-consistent-zero-shot-imitation.tldr: CIRL learns to infer goals from single demonstrations and pursue them without test-time interaction or updates, accounting for differences in goal difficulty.

paragraphs: Forecasting long time series requires recognizing broad patterns while remaining sensitive to brief local changes. In medical signals, those changes can indicate pathological events. This paper identifies a problem with architectures that use separate global and local branches: the branches can learn similar representations, reducing their ability to distinguish local variations from the larger pattern.

The proposed Dual-Stream Enhancement Mechanism changes the structure of learning to increase the distinction between global and local patterns. It allows weak interactions between the streams while alleviating excessively strong feature coupling. The purpose is to make the two branches provide more complementary information rather than repeatedly describing similar aspects of the signal.

The authors build DSENet around this mechanism for blood glucose prediction. They report state-of-the-art performance on multiple public datasets alongside extremely low computational cost. These findings support separating global and local representations as a useful forecasting design in the evaluated settings. The proposed use of DSENet as a baseline in additional domains remains a future application opportunity.
icml-2026-dsenet-a-novel-dual-stream-enh.tldr: DSENet improves blood glucose forecasting by keeping global trends and local variations more distinct within a low-cost dual-stream architecture.

paragraphs: Large populations of neurons can exhibit collective activity that is approximately low-dimensional. Finding a compact representation could therefore make their behavior easier to study. However, compressing observations without considering time can distort their dynamics, while latent dynamical models can permit several different underlying dynamics to explain the same observations.

This paper introduces a flow-matching approach with two coordinated flow fields. One describes how activity evolves over time; the other maps between observations and a smaller latent space. The compression flow is trained to minimize distortion of temporal dynamics, yielding an identifiable representation that preserves temporal relationships in the original data.

The method also uses a soft, parameterized constraint to encourage low-dimensional support, drawing inspiration from nested dropout. Across neural and behavioral datasets, the authors report more interpretable dynamics and better reconstructions than competing models. This includes noise-dominated datasets where conventional approaches fail. The contribution is therefore a form of compression designed to retain the time-dependent structure that makes these recordings scientifically useful.
icml-2026-dynamic-compression-flows-for-.tldr: A dual-flow model compresses neural and behavioral recordings while preserving temporal relationships, improving interpretability and reconstruction in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains models across devices without collecting their data centrally. Explaining those models introduces another coordination problem: explanations should reflect each client’s model while remaining consistent across clients. Existing approaches can leave explanations isolated, require substantial or sensitive communication, or sacrifice predictive accuracy by replacing expressive models with simpler ones.

xFedAlign separates task-model training from explanation coordination. Each client distills a lightweight surrogate and produces compact, private attribution summaries containing its top-ranked contributions for each class. The server robustly aggregates these summaries into a Global Explanation Prior. This prior softly aligns local explanations without constraining learning of the task model.

Across image, text, and tabular benchmarks with both similar and heterogeneous client distributions, xFedAlign matches FedAvg accuracy while reducing explanation drift and improving deletion and insertion AUC against the stated explanation baselines. Communication increases by only a few kilobytes per round. Additional evaluations show reduced membership-inference advantage and greater resistance to attribution poisoning, supporting the framework’s explanation consistency, privacy, and robustness in the tested settings.
icml-2026-explainable-federated-learning.tldr: xFedAlign coordinates compact explanation summaries across federated clients, improving explanation consistency while matching FedAvg accuracy in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Image dehazing aims to recover clear scene content from photographs obscured by atmospheric haze. Training on synthetic haze can transfer poorly to real scenes, while collecting real hazy images may expose a model to only a limited range of conditions. This paper proposes a framework trained without any hazy images.

Its central ingredient is a set of representations designed to remain unchanged between clean and hazy versions of images. The authors derive these representations theoretically and validate them experimentally. They then train a conditional diffusion model using clean images and their invariant representations, learning to generate clear content from information that can also be extracted through haze.

At test time, representations extracted from a hazy image guide the diffusion model toward the clean-image distribution. This connects hazy inputs to clean-image training through a shared representation. Quantitative analyses support the representations’ effectiveness, and experiments across real-world haze datasets report significant improvements over existing methods. The findings support generalization beyond the haze conditions that a conventional training collection would provide.
icml-2026-fully-zero-shot-image-dehazing.tldr: A diffusion dehazing framework learns entirely from clean images by conditioning on representations shared by clean and hazy scenes.

paragraphs: A proactive language-model assistant must decide what information to request and when it has enough to stop asking. Optimizing isolated conversational turns or training against simulated users can leave a gap between learned behavior and real interactions. Learn-to-Ask instead learns questioning policies from existing conversations conducted by experts.

The framework uses the observed continuation of each expert conversation to assign informative rewards to individual turns. These rewards are intended to capture how a question contributes to the expert’s longer-term strategy. Policy learning becomes a sequence of supervised learning tasks covering both question selection and stopping. An automated prompt-calibration pipeline uses minimal human supervision to improve generated rewards and sampling quality.

Across multiple datasets and model scales, the authors report consistent gains in proactive information seeking. They also describe a large-scale deployment in which the trained agent surpasses an internal expert baseline under professional audit. This supplies real-world evidence for the framework and supports the proposed rewards as a useful proxy for proactivity in that deployment.
icml-2026-grounded-in-reality-learning-a.tldr: Learn-to-Ask uses the recorded futures of expert conversations to train better questioning and stopping policies without user simulators.

paragraphs: When only a few examples are available for a new task, evaluations on related benchmarks offer potentially useful evidence about which models to trust. The difficulty is deciding what those earlier results actually imply. This paper studies a task-relatedness assumption that can connect benchmark performance to provable benefits on a new task.

The assumption is approximate weak monotonicity: a model that dominates another across many benchmarks tends to perform better on the new task as well. The authors observe this tendency empirically and analyze learning under both weak monotonicity and its approximate form. The relationship is a qualified tendency, so its usefulness depends on how well it describes the tasks being considered.

The analysis covers transfer learning and model selection aggregation. Benchmark information can eliminate parts of the model class, but the authors show that it can also inform adaptation to the geometry of the remaining tradeoffs. Their frontier-based approach therefore uses more than a simple ranking: it exploits the structure of available performance compromises when new-task evidence is scarce.
icml-2026-hedging-on-the-frontier-learni.tldr: Under approximate weak monotonicity, benchmark results can guide few-sample learning through model pruning and adaptation to available performance tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Disease progression involves information that hospital-event sequences alone do not capture, including organ measurements and social determinants of health. This paper develops DiffDT to bring these sources into a generative model for simulated disease reasoning. Social determinants enter through ICD-coded proxies, linking their digital representation to healthcare histories and sensor-derived measurements.

The framework uses conditioned latent diffusion to connect multi-organ data with tokenized healthcare events. A geometric diffusion component models the temporal evolution of brain networks, represented as graphs of connections between regions. Parallel diffusion models handle tabular measurements from other organ systems. Integrating these components with social-determinant proxies supports simulated interventions and reasoning about future disease trajectories.

Experiments use UK Biobank data covering brain, heart, liver, and kidney imaging traits alongside nearly 500,000 medical-history sequences. The authors report significant improvements over disease autoregressive models and imaging-trait generative baselines. These results support the integrated modeling approach on that dataset; the intervention component concerns in silico simulation using the modeled proxies.
icml-2026-marrying-generative-model-of-h.tldr: DiffDT combines multi-organ measurements, healthcare histories, and coded social-determinant proxies to improve simulated disease-trajectory modeling.

paragraphs: Reference-guided video editing combines a source video, a written instruction, and a reference image. The model must apply the requested change while retaining motion and untouched content. Processing language and imagery separately can create a mismatch between their representations, but using only a unified model’s final layer can discard spatial details needed for precise edits.

MiVE draws on the observation that different vision-language model layers provide complementary information. Earlier layers capture localized details, while deeper layers represent broader meaning useful for interpreting instructions. The framework extracts features across layers of Qwen3-VL and integrates them into a diffusion transformer using unified self-attention.

This architecture gives the editor access to both spatial detail and instruction-level meaning, addressing the modality mismatch associated with the cross-attention designs discussed in the paper. In the reported experiments, MiVE achieves the highest human preference ranking and outperforms academic methods and commercial systems. The findings support using a hierarchy of vision-language features for editing tasks that need both precise visual placement and semantic understanding.
icml-2026-mive-multiscale-vision-languag.tldr: MiVE combines features from multiple vision-language model layers to improve reference-guided video editing and achieves the highest reported human preference ranking.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text through a denoising process, during which input distributions and generation difficulty change. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adapting these models, but standard LoRA uses static adaptation parameters. This paper argues that ignoring the current noise level leaves those adaptations poorly matched to the changing demands of generation.

NaRA introduces a low-rank core matrix produced by a lightweight hypernetwork conditioned on noise level. The hypernetwork is shared globally, allowing the adaptation matrices to vary continuously throughout denoising without requiring a separate full adaptation for every stage. The authors describe the additional parameter and latency costs as negligible.

The paper provides a theoretical justification and evaluates the method on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and code generation benchmarks. It reports consistent improvements over noise-agnostic baselines across these tasks. The findings support making the fine-tuning mechanism responsive to diffusion progress, so that a compact adaptation can change with the type of input the model is currently processing.
icml-2026-nara-noise-aware-lora-for-para.tldr: NaRA makes low-rank adaptations depend on diffusion noise level, improving reasoning and code generation with negligible reported overhead.

paragraphs: A navigation policy trained on fixed demonstrations can encounter unfamiliar situations once its own actions determine where it goes. Errors may then compound. NavOL addresses this distribution shift by collecting expert labels during the policy’s simulated rollouts, allowing training examples to reflect situations the policy actually visits.

Starting from a pretrained diffusion policy that maps local observations to future waypoints, NavOL alternates between rollout and update phases. During rollout, a global planner with privileged environmental access supplies optimal path segments as labels. During update, the policy learns from the resulting observation–trajectory pairs. This supplies direct supervision without requiring a designed reward function.

The system uses IsaacLab, parallel rendering, and randomization of camera poses and start–goal pairs. Across 50 scenes on eight RTX 4090 GPUs, it collects over 2,000 trajectories per hour, averaging more than 400 steps each. The authors also introduce an indoor navigation benchmark and report consistent gains in simulation and real-world experiments, supporting online imitation as an effective navigation-training approach.
icml-2026-navol-navigation-policy-with-o.tldr: NavOL improves navigation through simulated rollout–update cycles that obtain expert path labels for situations visited by the policy itself.

paragraphs: Dilated attention reduces attention computation and key–value cache size while retaining long-range connections. However, directly imposing this sparse pattern on a pretrained attention model can severely damage accuracy. RAT+ changes dense pretraining so that one model can later support several sparse inference configurations with a short adaptation.

The architecture augments attention with full-sequence recurrence and active recurrence learning. After dense pretraining, it can switch to dilated attention, optionally include local windows, or mix configurations across layers and heads. The transition requires a one-billion-token resolution adaptation, avoiding the need to train a separate sparse model from scratch for each configuration.

At 1.5 billion parameters and 100 billion training tokens, RAT+ closely matches dense accuracy at dilation 16 and loses about two to three points at dilation 64 on the stated tasks. Larger experiments at 2.6 and 7.6 billion parameters include a one-point average accuracy loss with 64-fold reductions in attention FLOPs and cache size. These reductions concern the attention components measured in the paper.
icml-2026-rat-train-dense-infer-sparse-r.tldr: RAT+ combines dense attention pretraining with recurrence to support substantially sparser inference after a short adaptation, with modest reported accuracy losses.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning adapts vision-language models across medical-data clients, commonly by tuning text while freezing the visual encoder. This relies on visual features already separating relevant categories. The authors argue that medical images can violate this assumption because similar morphology compresses feature diversity and differing acquisition protocols create inconsistent feature geometry across clients.

FedMAP addresses these issues by restructuring the visual representation through Visual Manifold Anchoring. An LLM-derived codebook provides a shared synchronization signal that is invariant across clients. Manifold Semantic Anchoring and Topology Structural Alignment use this signal to organize the visual space and enforce consistent relationships between classes.

The authors evaluate FedMAP on FedISIC, FedCamelyon17, and a private ultrasound dataset. They report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, particularly under high noise, where the identified feature collapse is most severe. The findings support addressing the visual geometry itself when adapting these models to medical imaging, with a shared semantic reference helping coordinate clients whose image-acquisition conditions differ.
icml-2026-rethinking-federated-prompt-le.tldr: FedMAP uses a shared LLM-derived codebook to restructure medical-image features and align class relationships across federated clients.

paragraphs: Large language models require substantial storage and movement of model weights. When inference is limited by memory access, reducing the information transferred to compute units can improve speed. S-Quant tackles this by compressing weights through a representation that regenerates parts of each weight block from a compact seed.

The method partitions weight tensors into fixed-size blocks. Each block receives a seed that drives a hardware-friendly Linear Feedback Shift Register generator, producing several basis matrices. Block-specific coefficients combine these matrices to reconstruct the weights. Storing seeds and coefficients substantially reduces the stored data and improves transfer efficiency between memory and computation.

Experiments on language models ranging from seven to 70 billion parameters report state-of-the-art performance at approximately three-bit and four-bit weight compression. The authors also design a dedicated ASIC accelerator and report a fourfold speedup for memory-bound inference. The contribution joins a compact weight representation with hardware designed to regenerate it efficiently; the stated acceleration applies to the memory-bound setting.
icml-2026-s-quant-rethinking-weight-quan.tldr: S-Quant reconstructs weight blocks from seeded basis matrices and coefficients, delivering strong low-bit results and a fourfold memory-bound inference speedup on its ASIC.

paragraphs: Pretraining usually aims to produce the strongest base model, assuming that strength will carry through later adaptation. This paper examines another factor: the geometry around the learned parameters. A model’s location in the optimization landscape influences how much its existing capability survives subsequent updates or quantization.

The authors study three approaches that favor flatter minima: Sharpness-Aware Minimization, larger learning rates, and shorter learning-rate annealing periods. Flatter regions make the geometry around a solution less sharply sensitive to parameter changes. Across models with 20 million to 150 million parameters, these interventions consistently improve performance after post-training on five datasets, with up to 80% less forgetting.

The paper also tests a short Sharpness-Aware Minimization phase on an existing OLMo-2-1B checkpoint. It reduces forgetting by 31% after MetaMath post-training and by 40% after four-bit quantization. These findings support evaluating pretraining choices partly by how well capabilities survive later changes, rather than assessing the base checkpoint only at the moment pretraining ends.
icml-2026-sharpness-aware-pretraining-mi.tldr: Pretraining interventions that favor flatter minima reduce reported forgetting after post-training and quantization, including in an existing billion-parameter checkpoint.

paragraphs: Flow-based generative models can supply useful prior knowledge for reconstructing images from incomplete or degraded measurements. The challenge is guiding their generation toward a result consistent with those measurements. Existing optimal-control formulations can require expensive trajectory optimization, including differentiation through the flow dynamics or solving adjoint systems.

MPC-Flow divides this guidance problem into a sequence of smaller control subproblems using model predictive control. The authors connect the resulting procedure theoretically to the underlying optimal-control objective. Different algorithmic choices produce a range of guidance methods, including regimes that avoid backpropagating through the generative trajectory.

The method is evaluated on linear and nonlinear image-restoration problems, including inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution. The authors report strong performance and demonstrate training-free guidance of a quantized, 32-billion-parameter FLUX.2 model on consumer hardware. This supports the practicality of the control formulation at substantial model scale, with the hardware demonstration specifically relying on a quantized setting. The approach applies guidance during inference without additional model training.
icml-2026-solving-inverse-problems-with-.tldr: MPC-Flow makes training-free image-restoration guidance practical by splitting flow-model optimal control into successive smaller problems.

paragraphs: Combining trained LoRA adapters can bring multiple generative capabilities into one diffusion model, but their parameter updates can interfere destructively. SSR-Merge addresses this by controlling how internal signals move through the combined adapters. Its central proposal is to resolve conflicting contributions through signal routing instead of merging parameters directly.

The method first concatenates candidate adapters along their rank dimension to construct a shared subspace. An inverse correlation matrix then separates correlated contributions within that space. A directional guide matrix routes the resulting signals toward their corresponding task-specific subspaces. These stages aim to preserve distinct capabilities while allowing the adapters to operate together.

The authors prove that SSR aligns with an Ordinary Least Squares solution, establishing mathematical optimality in that formulation. They also exploit additive sufficient statistics to create a streaming algorithm that supports on-the-fly updates with reduced memory and computation. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art merging methods while maintaining comparable efficiency, supporting signal routing as an effective way to manage adapter interference.
icml-2026-ssr-merge-subspace-signal-rout.tldr: SSR-Merge combines diffusion-model LoRAs through decorrelated signal routing, reducing interference with an Ordinary Least Squares foundation and streaming updates.

paragraphs: Sparse attention often saves time by fetching fewer keys from memory. This paper examines settings involving Multi-head Latent Attention and Multi-Token Prediction where decoding attention instead becomes limited by computation. In that regime, selecting keys alone can waste work because different query heads need different interactions with each retrieved key.

TileSparse evaluates sparsity using a cost model centered on compute tile size rather than the number of fetched tokens. Its two-dimensional query-head–key sparsity removes unnecessary head–key calculations and spends the freed compute on retrieving more semantically important tokens. A tiered variant and an automatic tuner adapt the pattern to differences in query-head sparsity across keys.

Under tight budgets, experiments report a 40% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art dynamic key-only sparse methods. The method also retains 99% of full-attention accuracy while reducing attention computation by 40.8%. These findings show why the relevant bottleneck matters: when computation is scarce, choosing which head–key interactions to calculate can use the budget more effectively than selecting keys alone.
icml-2026-tilesparse-arithmetic-intensit.tldr: TileSparse prunes query-head–key interactions to improve accuracy per compute budget in compute-bound language-model decoding.

paragraphs: Understanding a photograph’s setting involves more than recognizing its location. A model may also need to infer the season, time of day, or whether spatial and temporal clues fit together physically. TimeSpot evaluates this broader ability using visual evidence alone, extending beyond location recognition from landmarks and road signs.

The benchmark contains 1,455 ground-level images from 80 countries. It requests structured predictions of temporal attributes, including season, month, time of day, and daylight phase. Geographic predictions include continent, country, climate zone, environment type, and coordinates. Additional reasoning tasks test physical plausibility while accounting for the uncertainty present in real-world images.

Evaluations of leading open- and closed-source vision-language models show low performance, especially on temporal inference. Supervised fine-tuning improves results, but the authors find the resulting performance still insufficient. The benchmark therefore exposes weaknesses in connecting visual cues to time and physical context, even when models can recognize geographic information. Its tasks provide a way to assess progress on these related capabilities together.
icml-2026-timespot-benchmarking-geo-temp.tldr: TimeSpot tests location, time, and physical-context inference from images, revealing especially weak temporal understanding in evaluated vision-language models.

paragraphs: Treatment responder classification aims to identify individuals who would benefit from a treatment. This paper allows the classifier to abstain when it is uncertain, leaving some individuals for further investigation. That changes the learning problem: a useful rule must balance classification errors against how often it declines to decide.

The authors connect causal misclassification risk with abstention to Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR. This relationship leads to TRECA, a doubly robust method for learning the classification rule under loose convergence conditions on nuisance parameters. The method therefore incorporates both causal estimation and the option to withhold a classification within the same learning framework.

The paper further extends the approach to handle possible violations of assumptions including monotonicity and unconfoundedness. Theoretical analysis and experiments on two real-world datasets support learning rules with low regret while using limited abstention. The contribution is a principled way to reserve uncertain cases for additional investigation, with the stated guarantees and extensions tied to the causal learning setting studied.
icml-2026-treatment-responder-classifica.tldr: TRECA learns treatment-benefit classification rules that can abstain on uncertain cases, using a connection between causal classification risk and CVaR.

paragraphs: Image–text relationships can have degrees of similarity, yet many training datasets label pairs only as matches or nonmatches. This can treat partially related pairs as false negatives and encourage a model to fit distinctions that are too coarse. The paper identifies this annotation problem as a source of poor cross-modal generalization.

VACSR reformulates learning from such limited semantic annotations as a variational inference problem. It builds a latent representation of cross-modal similarity and applies regularization to reduce overfitting to binary labels. The aim is to represent a richer similarity structure despite the restricted supervision available in the dataset.

The authors distinguish this approach from methods focused primarily on ambiguity within an individual modality, which can overlook problems in the matching annotations themselves. Experiments cover image–text retrieval, domain generalization, and generalization from base classes to novel classes. The reported results support the adapter’s effectiveness across these settings, suggesting that explicitly accommodating coarse matching labels can improve how learned similarities transfer beyond the training data.
icml-2026-variational-adapter-for-cross-.tldr: VACSR models latent image–text similarity to reduce overfitting to coarse binary annotations and improve cross-modal generalization.

paragraphs: In a single-stream autoregressive interface, generated tokens both influence subsequent generation and become public commitments. Waiting to finish deliberation delays useful content, while speaking too early can commit the model to claims that bias later reasoning. This paper treats the timing of disclosure as something a model can learn to control.

Side-by-Side Interleaved Reasoning alternates partial public answers with continued private reasoning in the same context. Its training trajectories align answer prefixes with reasoning prefixes that support them, encouraging useful disclosures instead of filler. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the two action types, and reinforcement learning recovers reasoning performance under the interleaved format.

The authors evaluate two Qwen3 models, a mixture-of-experts model and a smaller dense model, on AIME25 and GPQA-Diamond. They report better tradeoffs between accuracy and content latency under token-level proxies such as waiting between updates. The evidence supports improved pacing of substantive content under those measures; it specifically concerns proxy-based latency rather than a stated wall-clock speed improvement.
icml-2026-when-to-think-when-to-speak-le.tldr: Side-by-Side trains models to disclose supported answer portions during continued reasoning, improving measured accuracy–content-latency tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can understand an image broadly while missing small details that determine the answer to a question. Repeatedly zooming into relevant regions can help, but requires extra tool calls and visual encoding during inference. This paper moves the benefit of close inspection into the training process.

Region-to-Image Distillation first gives strong teacher models tightly cropped image regions so they can generate high-quality visual question-answering data. The resulting supervision is then distilled into a smaller student using the full image. The student learns from answers grounded in local evidence while practicing the full-image perception required at deployment.

The authors also introduce ZoomBench, covering six fine-grained perceptual dimensions, with a dual-view protocol that measures the performance gap between global and regional views. Experiments report leading results across multiple fine-grained perception benchmarks and improvements in broader tasks such as visual reasoning and GUI agents. The trained student obtains these perception gains in a single forward pass without inference-time zooming tools.
icml-2026-zooming-without-zooming-region.tldr: Region-to-Image Distillation transfers supervision from zoomed-in teacher views to full-image students, improving fine-grained perception without inference-time tools.
